newsitem.title: USA: US senator's electricity bill wins guarded welcome.
newsitem.headline: US senator's electricity bill wins guarded welcome.

text.p: U.S. Senator Dale Bumpers drew guarded praise Thursday from power producers and industrial power consumers with a bill to open electricity markets to competition across the United States before 2004.

The Arkansas Democrat's proposal was the first of what is expected to be a long list of bills in Congress this year to break up utility monopolies over power supplies to homes, businesses and industry.
Investor-owned utilities, independent power producers, and big manufacturers hailed the bill for covering all of the main issues linked to overhauling the industry.
"A lot of this bill is very commendable," said Paul J. Allen, spokesman for the Alliance for Competitive Electricity, a group of investor-owned utilities pushing for competition.
The legislation called for all electricity consumers to be able to shop for power by December 15, 2003.
It would assure utilities "stranded cost" recovery -- recovery in their rates of the costs of assets that would become unprofitable as customers switched to other suppliers.
But it said states could force utilities to sell off power plants in order to limit stranded costs to the difference between the sale price and book value of the assets.
The Edison Electric Institute (EEI), which represents the majority of investor-owned utilities, said it was "very concerned" about the power plant divestiture provision.
"We think that would set up a fire sale of generating plants," said EEI spokeswoman Mary Kenkel.

"If you're selling them all at the same time, the chances are you're going to get less to cover what's on the books," which Kenkel said would increase the amount of stranded costs that would be imposed on customers.

Big industrial consumers were leery about the stranded cost provision. John Anderson, executive director of the Electricity Consumers Resource Council, said it would have been better to leave the decision on stranded costs totally up to states.

Chemical Manufacturers' Association said the bill would "force all consumers -- big and small, residentail and business -- to pay for the mistakes and poor management decisions of electric utilities."
But industrial consumers' biggest concern was that the deadline for competition was too far in the future.
Chemical manufacturers said the deadline should be no later than January 2000 or two years after a bill is passed.
Municipal power suppliers and rural electric cooperatives, who would have to compete with investor-owned utilities under Bumpers' proposal, were less sanguine about any deadline.
"We can't support any bill that includes a federal mandate that would preempt state and local community decision-making," said Madeline Cafruny, spokeswoman for the American Public Power Association.

While liking the proposal to put municipal and investor-owned utilities on the same footing, big utilities said it was unfair that the Tennessee Valley Authority would be allowed to sell power outside its territory without taking away its public subsidies.
Small business and residential consumers were pleased that Bumpers addressed the need for a universal service guarantee in areas where there would be no competition.

Bumpers bill called for the government to study what impact competition in the power market would have on air pollution and recommend by 2000 changes in clean air rules, if necessary, to protect public health and the environment.

The bill also called for the repeal of the Public Utility Holding Company Act, which restricts business activities of some multi-state utilities, and the Public Utility Regulatory Policy Act, which requires utilities to buy a certain amount of power from co-generators and power producers that use renewable energy.
--Sonali Paul, (202) 898 8320
